messages.content: Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

The Bookings API covers appointments on one or more calendars: creating them, moving them, cancelling them, and asking what time is still free.

Everything runs over HTTPS and speaks JSON. There are four resources you will use constantly. A *calendar* is the thing being booked — a room, a person, a piece of equipment. An *availability rule* describes when that calendar is open, in recurring weekly terms plus whatever exceptions you add for holidays. A *booking* is a confirmed slot held on a calendar. An *attendee* is someone attached to a booking, with their own notification preferences.

Two things trip people up early, so they are worth stating here. First, every timestamp you send or receive is UTC in RFC 3339 format, and each calendar carries its own IANA timezone for display. Converting is your job, not ours. Second, bookings are created against a version token returned by the availability endpoint. If someone else takes the slot between your read and your write, the write fails with a 409 rather than double-booking. Retry the read, then the write.

Authentication uses bearer tokens scoped per calendar. Rate limits are documented per endpoint and returned in response headers on every call.

The next section walks through booking a single slot end to end.

The Bookings API handles appointments across one or many calendars: booking them, rescheduling them, cancelling them, and asking what time is still open.

Everything travels over HTTPS as JSON. Four resources come up again and again. A *calendar* is whatever gets booked: a room, a person, a machine. An *availability rule* says when that calendar is open, expressed as a recurring weekly pattern plus any exceptions you add for holidays. A *booking* is a confirmed slot held against a calendar. An *attendee* is a person attached to a booking, carrying their own notification preferences.

Two details catch people out early, so we will say them up front. Every timestamp you send or receive is UTC in RFC 3339 format, and each calendar stores its own IANA timezone for display. Conversion is on you, not on us. And bookings are written against a version token that the availability endpoint hands back. If another client claims the slot between your read and your write, the write returns 409 instead of double-booking. Read again, then write again.

Authentication is by bearer token, scoped to a calendar. Rate limits are listed per endpoint and echoed in response headers on every call.

The section that follows walks a single booking from start to finish.

The Bookings API manages appointments on a single calendar or many: creating them, moving them, cancelling them, and asking what time remains open.

Everything moves over HTTPS in JSON. Four resources will become familiar fast. A *calendar* is the thing being reserved — a room, a person, a piece of equipment. An *availability rule* defines when that calendar is open, as a repeating weekly pattern plus whatever exceptions you add for holidays. A *booking* is a confirmed slot held on a calendar. An *attendee* is someone attached to a booking, along with their own notification preferences.

Two points cause most early confusion, so here they are. Every timestamp you send or receive is UTC in RFC 3339 format, while each calendar keeps its own IANA timezone for display. The conversion belongs to you, not to us. Also, bookings are created against a version token that the availability endpoint returns. If a different client takes the slot between your read and your write, the write comes back 409 rather than double-booking. Read once more, then write.

Authentication runs on bearer tokens, scoped per calendar. Rate limits are documented endpoint by endpoint and repeated in response headers on every call.

The next section takes one booking through the whole flow.
